summary: Race-by-race Model Talk comparing FLIPR (75 percent Democratic Senate odds) with Polymarket (about two-thirds), whose race-level odds correlate 0.99 with FLIPR's. Silver argues the disagreement is about individual races, not overall uncertainty, and that markets may over-tighten late and lean on early voting, which FLIPR ignores. He flags where FLIPR may be wrong: no ideology variable for non-incumbents (Michigan), past margins credited only to incumbents (Ohio's Brown, Alaska's Peltola), ranked-choice effects (Alaska), lagging partisan lean from domestic migration (Florida), and inelastic states (Mississippi, Louisiana, South Carolina). He also covers how internal polls and independents are treated, and lists simple-fundamentals values for the red-state tranche.

findings.statement: The point of building a model is to set clear rules ahead of time so you do not rely on gut or ad hoc mid-stream assumptions; FLIPR gives an independent daily opinion from rules locked months earlier. Silver keeps a list of possible changes for next cycle rather than making subjective in-season adjustments.
findings.rationale: Avoid hedging and herding during 'silly season'.
findings.evidence_quote: the whole point of building a model, in some sense, is to set clear rules ahead of time so you don’t have to trust your gut or make ad hoc assumptions in midstream.

findings.statement: On Oct. 25, 2026 FLIPR and Polymarket Senate race probabilities correlated at 0.99. Silver estimates that plugging Polymarket's race odds into FLIPR's correlation structure would yield 65 to 70 percent for Democrats, close to Polymarket's topline, versus FLIPR's 75, so the disagreement is about individual races, not total uncertainty. FLIPR appeared to lead markets by a couple of days after Labor Day, and markets may have reacted to FLIPR's launch.
findings.evidence_quote: Overall, there’s far more agreement than disagreement; the correlation coefficient is .99.

findings.statement: FLIPR does not use early-voting data, except insofar as pollsters' assumptions about early voting are reflected in polls. Silver is skeptical of early-vote analysis, though Joel Wertheimer argues it can help if focused on which party turns out unlikely voters.
findings.evidence_quote: markets may be building in some information — or assumptions — based on early voting data, something that FLIPR doesn’t really look at.

findings.statement: Prediction markets tend to become more confident as elections approach. Silver argues this misapplies the time-decay principle: late in a modern midterm most uncertainty is whether polls were right all along, which does not shrink until results arrive, and FLIPR assumes little late poll movement, an assumption tweaked in the 2026 rebuild.
findings.evidence_quote: Most of the remaining uncertainty in the race isn’t about how polls will change over the final week-and-a-half, but rather about whether there will be another major polling error again

findings.statement: With a D+9.5 likely-voter generic ballot (about a 12-point swing from 2024), FLIPR's simple fundamentals for the red-state tranche were: Alaska R+0.2, Florida R+1.1, Iowa R+1.2 (about R+1), Ohio R+1.6, Texas R+1.9, with a big gap to Kansas (blended R+4.4). Minnesota was D+13 in the generic-ballot baseline.
findings.evidence_quote: Alaska is only R +0.2, Florida R +1.1, Iowa R +1.2, Ohio R +1.6, and Texas R +1.9.

findings.statement: Because fancy fundamentals credit past winning margins only to incumbents, FLIPR may underrate strong non-incumbent candidates with 'proof of concept': Sherrod Brown (won Ohio by almost 7 in 2018, lost by only 3.6 in 2024 while outrunning Harris) and Mary Peltola. Races with appointed incumbents, like Husted in Ohio, are treated as open seats.
findings.evidence_quote: Our “fancy fundamentals” calculation incorporates past winning margins for incumbents, although not for non-incumbents like Brown.

findings.statement: FLIPR lacks a mechanism for a non-incumbent's ideology; in Michigan, El-Sayed's fundraising made fancy fundamentals better than his polls, and Silver thinks accounting for his ideology would bring FLIPR close to Polymarket.
findings.evidence_quote: FLIPR doesn’t really have any mechanism to account for El-Sayed’s progressivism, even though I think it would be reasonable to do so.

findings.statement: Whenever polls and fundamentals disagree, FLIPR raises the race's uncertainty; for example Minnesota had an 11 percent chance of a Republican win and was the tipping point 7 percent of the time despite a D+13 baseline.
findings.evidence_quote: Whenever there’s a disagreement between polls and “fundamentals,” uncertainty tends to be higher, and FLIPR accounts for this.

findings.statement: Internal campaign polls carry a typical 3 to 4-point bias toward their sponsor, so in FLIPR logic a Republican internal showing the Republican up only 2 is evidence of a toss-up, and a candidate's own internal showing him up 1 is worse news for him than opposing internals showing him down 2 or 3.
findings.evidence_quote: In FLIPR logic, that’s actually a worse poll for him than Republican internals showing him trailing by 2 or 3.

findings.statement: In Florida, partisan lean scores lag reality because domestic migrants are heavily Republican and voter registration keeps trending red. Silver names accounting for domestic migration trends in partisan lean as one of the more obvious future model improvements.
findings.evidence_quote: One of the more obvious improvements in our model in future years would be to account for these domestic migration trends in our partisan lean scores.

findings.statement: Highly inelastic states with few swing voters, such as Louisiana, Mississippi and South Carolina with large Black populations and conservative evangelical whites, make big Democratic overperformance unlikely; Silver judged 3 to 5 percent more grounded than markets' 8 to 13 percent for Louisiana and Mississippi. New Hampshire, by contrast, is one of the most elastic states.
findings.evidence_quote: Louisiana and Mississippi are extremely inelastic states, with very few true swing voters.

findings.statement: FLIPR assumes independents Dan Osborn (Nebraska) and Seth Bodnar (Montana) would caucus with Democrats. Third-party candidates get asymmetric, feast-or-famine distributions. In Montana, a three-way race with a Democrat taking 22.5 percent, the forecast is assumption-driven and volatile, hinging on tactical voting.
findings.evidence_quote: FLIPR builds in some slightly complex assumptions about third-party candidates in cases like this, seeing them as having asymmetric distributions that are a little bit feast-or-famine.

findings.statement: Alaska and Maine are among the states least correlated with national outcomes, so a party can win them on a bad night or lose them on a good one.
findings.evidence_quote: Alaska, up in the Arctic Circle, is one of the least correlated states with the Lower 48.

political_insights.insight: Predicted Democratic suburban gains in Texas were offset by Trump's gains with working-class Latinos in South Texas, which 2026 polls suggest may reverse.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: Subgroup trend reversals can swing state baselines quickly.

political_insights.insight: Kansas is trending slightly blue relative to the nation (Clinton -21 in 2016, Harris -16 in 2024), with Democratic wins in KS-3, governor races and the 2022 abortion referendum.

references.description: Joel Wertheimer on early voting data

open_questions: Whether FLIPR will add a non-incumbent ideology variable or past-margin credit for former officeholders in future versions.
